label: Child car seats
title: Child passengers
headline: The right seat, fitted right
intro: A child in a car needs more than a lap or an adult belt. See how a child seat protects them, and how to check it's done right.

contentNotice.text: This experience talks about children being hurt in crashes. It uses simple diagrams, not images of children.

scenes.question: Child restraints cut deaths among infants in crashes by about how much?

lines: You're driving your sister's toddler home. The child seat is in the back, but it was put in quickly.
It moves when you push it, and the straps are a bit loose.

art.alt: Side view of a child seat on the back seat of a car.

scenes.prompt: The seat is loose. What should you do before driving?

art.alt: A loosely fitted child seat tipped forward.

options.label: Tighten and check the fitted restraints
options.reason: Follow the seat and vehicle instructions. Check the approved belt or anchors and top tether, where required, before every trip.

options.label: Leave it loose for a short trip
options.reason: A short trip still needs a correctly fitted restraint.

scenes.prompt: A car brakes hard in front of you. Compare a seat fitted loosely and one fitted firmly.

art.alt: Side view of a child seat on a rear seat during a sudden stop.

states.label: Loose
states.caption: A loose seat lurches forward and the child goes with it.

states.label: Firm
states.caption: Fitted firmly, the seat barely moves and holds the child in place.

scenes.prompt: Now the harness. Compare loose straps with straps done up snugly.

art.alt: Side view of a child in a harnessed seat during a sudden stop.

states.label: Loose straps
states.caption: With slack in the straps, the child slides forward and can come out of them.

states.label: Snug straps
states.caption: Snug straps keep the child in the seat's protective shell.

scenes.explain: Child restraints cut deaths among infants by about {claim:int.who.child-infant}. But {claim:na.stat.child-law}: Namibian law only requires one if the car has one, so it's up to you.

lines: Fit the seat so it moves no more than a little when you push it.
Do the harness up snugly every trip. You should only fit one finger under the straps.
Children ride in the back, in a seat that suits their size.

topics.title: Out of the booster
topics.blurb: When does an adult belt fit?

scenes.question: For seatbelt rules, Namibian law counts a person as an adult once they're taller than how many metres?

lines: Your nephew says he's too big for a booster seat now. He wants to sit on the back seat like an adult.

art.alt: Side view of a child on the back seat wearing an adult seatbelt.

scenes.prompt: An adult belt is made for an adult body. Compare where it sits on a child, with and without a booster.

art.alt: Side view of a child on a rear seat wearing an adult seatbelt.

states.label: No booster
states.caption: Without a booster the belt crosses the neck and the soft belly, where it can cause serious injury.

states.label: Booster
states.caption: A booster lifts the child so the belt crosses the shoulder and the hips instead.

art.alt: The child on the rear seat, with one point of the belt check highlighted at a time.

steps.title: Back against the seat
steps.body: Can they sit with their back right against the seat back?

steps.title: Knees bend at the edge
steps.body: Do their knees bend over the front of the seat?

steps.title: Belt across the shoulder
steps.body: Does the belt cross the middle of the shoulder, not the neck?

steps.title: Belt low on the hips
steps.body: Does the lap part sit low across the tops of the thighs, not the belly?

steps.title: Stays like that
steps.body: Can they sit like this for the whole trip? If not, they still need a booster.

scenes.explain: For seatbelt rules, someone taller than {claim:na.law.adult-height} or older than {claim:na.law.adult-age} counts as an adult. Being old enough isn't the same as the belt fitting: use the five-step check.

lines: Keep a child in a booster until the adult belt passes all five steps.
Every child must use a child seat or a belt, never your lap.
If there's no free belted seat, a child must sit in the back.

scenes.title: Just around the corner
scenes.label: A made-up story, based on common situations
scenes.warning: This story mentions a child being hurt. It doesn't describe the injury in detail.
paragraphs: Ndapewa was running late for school, so she put her son on the back seat without his booster. It was only around the corner.
A car pulled out in front of them and she braked hard. The belt slid up from his hips onto his belly.
He spent a week in hospital with bruising inside. 'He's fine now,' she says, 'but I'll never skip the booster again.'

signpost.text: If a crash has affected you or someone close to you, you don't have to deal with it alone. LifeLine/ChildLine Namibia offers free counselling: call {claim:na.support.lifeline}.
